etymology: Hebrew Ashdoth ha-Pisgah, “the springs (or slopes) of Pisgah”; the base and streams of the mountain range of Pisgah, east of Jordan overlooking the Salt Sea.
biblical_def: Ashdoth-pisgah, “the springs” or “slopes of Pisgah,” was the region at the foot of the Pisgah range, east of the Jordan, marking a boundary of the land given to the eastern tribes: “the plain also, and Jordan, and the coast thereof…under Ashdothpisgah eastward” (Deu 3:17). Pisgah is the mountain height from whose top Moses, at the end of his life, viewed the whole promised land which his eyes should see but his feet not enter, and where he died and was buried by the hand of God. Ashdoth-pisgah, the slopes and springs below that solemn summit, preaches the mingling of promise and chastening. From Pisgah Moses saw all the goodness God would give His people, yet was himself shut out for the sin at Meribah, that all Israel might learn how holy is the God who will be sanctified in them that come nigh Him. Yet the mercy is greater than the chastening: Moses, denied the earthly Canaan, was taken to the better country, and appeared centuries later on the mount of transfiguration in glory with the Lord. The slopes of Pisgah bid the believer look up in hope; though the earthly promise be withheld and the servant of God die outside the land, the true inheritance is not lost but exchanged for a better, the heavenly Canaan that no sin can bar to those whom grace has washed.

etymology: Hebrew Beth Haram, “house of the height” (also Beth-haran); a town of Gad in the Jordan valley, built by the Gadites.
biblical_def: Beth-haram, “the house of the height,” was a town of the tribe of Gad in the valley of the Jordan, among those the Gadites built when they received their inheritance east of the river: “And in the valley, Betharam, and Bethnimrah, and Succoth, and Zaphon” (Josh 13:27). It lay in the warm Jordan valley, a fertile and low-lying land, yet bore the name “house of the height.” The tribe of Gad was a warrior tribe, of whom Jacob said, a troop should overcome him, but he should overcome at the last, and Moses blessed him as a lion that teareth the arm with the crown of the head. Beth-haram, a “house of the height” in the low valley, preaches that the people of God are lifted up even in the low places. Though set in the valley of this world, the saints are raised up together and made to sit in heavenly places in Christ Jesus; their citizenship is in heaven, their affection set on things above. The name of the town bids the believer, though he dwell in the valley of humiliation, to lift up his heart, for he belongs to the house of the height. He is of the city that is above, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the lowest valley of his pilgrimage cannot lower the dignity God has given him in His Son.

etymology: Hebrew Ar, “a city”; the chief city of Moab on the Arnon, given by God to the children of Lot; distinct from Moab the nation.
biblical_def: Ar, or Ar of Moab, was the chief city of the Moabites, on the river Arnon, and it stands as a distinct place from Moab the nation whose capital it was. When the Amorites under Sihon came up out of Heshbon, they consumed it: “there is a fire gone out of Heshbon…it hath consumed Ar of Moab, and the lords of the high places of Arnon” (Num 21:28). Yet Israel was forbidden to seize it, for the LORD said, “Distress not the Moabites…because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession” (Deu 2:9). Here is a striking word: God had appointed even the Moabites, the sons of Lot, their portion, and He would not let Israel take it. Ar of Moab preaches the sovereignty of God over the lands of all peoples, and His faithfulness to His own appointments even toward those outside the covenant. He set the bounds of Moab as surely as the bounds of Israel; He gives to every nation its dwelling. Israel must respect the portion God had given the children of Lot, for the earth is the LORD’s and He divideth it as He will. Yet Moab, spared by Israel at God’s command, remained an enemy of His people and a worshipper of Chemosh, and the prophets pronounced her doom. Ar teaches both the wideness of God’s providence over the nations and the peril of a people who receive a portion from His hand yet will not own Him as Lord.

etymology: Hebrew Eglayim, “two pools” or “two calves”; a town of Moab, named in Isaiah’s lamentation over the land.
biblical_def: Eglaim was a town of Moab, named in the prophet Isaiah’s doleful oracle over that land: “For the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beerelim” (Isa 15:8). The whole burden of Moab is a lamentation: her cities laid waste in a night, her people weeping on the housetops, her mighty men crying out, the waters failing and the grass withered. Eglaim marks one bound of that howling, that the cry of Moab’s calamity reached even to its farthest towns. The oracle preaches the certainty and reach of God’s judgment upon a proud and idolatrous people. Moab was at ease from her youth, settled on her lees, lifted up in pride, and had not been emptied from vessel to vessel; therefore her taste remained in her and she was not changed. But the LORD sent a spoiler, and her howling went round about her borders unto Eglaim. Yet even in this oracle the prophet weeps: my heart shall cry out for Moab. The judgment of God is sure, but it is not without pity; and the reach of the howling unto Eglaim is a warning to every people at ease in their sin that the day of visitation will find out the farthest corner, and that pride and idolatry, though long spared, are surely brought down.

etymology: Hebrew Nimrim, perhaps “clear (or pure) waters”; the waters of Nimrim in Moab, named in the oracles of Isaiah and Jeremiah as made desolate.
biblical_def: The waters of Nimrim were streams and springs in the land of Moab, famed for their greenness and pasture, named in the lamentation over Moab as dried up in the day of judgment: “For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing” (Isa 15:6). Once these waters made a place of meadows and abundance; but when the LORD visited Moab for her pride and idolatry, the very waters failed, the grass withered, and the green thing was gone. Nimrim preaches the drying up of every earthly spring under the judgment of God. What a people trusts in for life and plenty — its waters, its harvests, its fat pastures — the LORD can wither in a day, that they may know their fatness was His gift and their idolatry their ruin. The green place became a desolation. So every fountain of earthly confidence fails at last; riches take wing, strength decays, the well runs dry. Only they who drink of the living water that Christ gives shall never thirst, for it is in them a well of water springing up into everlasting life. The desolate waters of Nimrim warn the soul not to hew out for itself broken cisterns, but to come to the fountain of living waters, which the LORD alone supplies and never suffers to fail.

etymology: Hebrew Tsophim, “watchers” or “place of the watchmen”; the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah, whither Balak brought Balaam to curse Israel.
biblical_def: The field of Zophim, “the field of the watchers,” was a high place on the top of Pisgah in Moab, one of the heights to which Balak the king of Moab brought Balaam the hireling prophet to curse Israel: “And he brought him into the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah, and built seven altars, and offered a bullock and a ram on every altar” (Num 23:14). From that watch-place, looking down on the tents of Israel spread in the plain, Balaam was constrained to bless where he was hired to curse, for God turned the curse into a blessing, and no enchantment could prevail against Jacob. Zophim, the field of the watchers, preaches the vanity of every device against the people of God. Balak spared no pains — height after height, altar upon altar, sacrifice upon sacrifice — yet the LORD would not suffer His people to be cursed, but put His own blessing in the mouth of the very prophet suborned to harm them. There is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel. From the watch-place of the enemy the word went forth: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob. The believer, though watched by malicious eyes and assailed by every stratagem of hell, is safe under the blessing of God, which no curse of man or devil can turn aside.

etymology: Hebrew Mattanah, “a gift”; a station of Israel’s wilderness journey east of the Arnon, on the way to the promised land.
biblical_def: Mattanah, “a gift,” was a station of Israel’s march through the wilderness, east of the Arnon, reached just after the song of the well: “the princes digged the well, the nobles of the people digged it…And from the wilderness they went to Mattanah” (Num 21:18). The LORD had bidden Israel gather at Beer, the well, and He gave them water; and they sang, Spring up, O well. From that place of the given water they journeyed on to Mattanah, whose very name means “gift.” The station preaches that all the way of God’s people is paved with gifts. The water in the desert was His gift, the manna His gift, the land before them His gift; every stage of the pilgrimage was marked by the free bounty of God, who gave and gave to an undeserving people. What have we that we did not receive? Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. Mattanah bids the traveller name his mercies and own them as gifts, not wages; for salvation itself is the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast. The believer journeys from gift to gift, sustained the whole way by grace, until he comes to the last and greatest gift, eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

etymology: Hebrew Nachaliel, “the torrent (or valley) of God”; a station of Israel’s wilderness journey between Mattanah and Bamoth.
biblical_def: Nahaliel, “the torrent of God,” was a station of Israel’s march toward the promised land, named between Mattanah and Bamoth: “And from Mattanah to Nahaliel: and from Nahaliel to Bamoth” (Num 21:19). The name joins the word for a brook or valley-stream with the name of God: it is God’s own torrent, a water-course given and owned by Him. Coming just after Mattanah, “the gift,” Nahaliel continues the theme of the LORD’s provision in the desert: from the gift to the torrent of God, the pilgrims were led from mercy to mercy. The name preaches the abundance and refreshment that God supplies to His people. There is a river, the streams whereof make glad the city of God; He gives His people to drink of the river of His pleasures, for with Him is the fountain of life. The torrent of God is no scanty trickle but a full stream of grace, that overflows to satisfy the thirsty in a dry land. So the Spirit is poured out as rivers of living water from the innermost being of the believer, and the redeemed drink deeply of the abundance of God. Nahaliel bids the pilgrim rejoice that his way runs beside the torrent of God, whose grace is a flowing river that fails not, and to drink and be satisfied all his journey through.

The principle to recover is the abundance of God’s refreshing grace. There is a river, the streams whereof make glad the city of God; He gives His people to drink of the river of His pleasures, for with Him is the fountain of life. The torrent of God is no scanty trickle but a full stream of grace. The Spirit is poured out as rivers of living water from the believer; let the pilgrim drink deeply, rejoicing that his way runs beside the torrent of God that fails not.

etymology: Hebrew Atad, “bramble” or “thorn”; the threshingfloor of Atad beyond Jordan, where Joseph and the Egyptians mourned for Jacob; afterward called Abel-mizraim.
biblical_def: The threshingfloor of Atad was a place beyond Jordan where the great funeral company of Joseph halted to mourn for his father Jacob on the way to bury him in the cave of Machpelah: “And they came to the threshingfloor of Atad, which is beyond Jordan, and there they mourned with a great and very sore lamentation: and he made a mourning for his father seven days” (Gen 50:10). The Canaanites who saw the mourning said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians; and the place was named Abel-mizraim, “the mourning of the Egyptians” (Gen 50:11). The name Atad means bramble or thorn, a fitting emblem for a place of grief, for thorns were the curse laid on the ground for man’s sin, and death and mourning are the fruit of that same fall. Atad preaches the reality and dignity of godly grief. Joseph did not despise to weep long and sorely for his father; the people of God mourn their dead, yet not as those who have no hope. The seven days’ lamentation at the bramble-floor gave way to the burial in the promised land, in the grave of the fathers, in sure hope of the resurrection. So the believer sorrows at the thorn-strewn floor of death, yet lifts his eyes beyond it to the land of promise, where the last enemy shall be destroyed, and God shall wipe away all tears, and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow nor crying.

etymology: Hebrew Ge-Melach, “the valley of salt”; a valley toward Edom, south of the Salt Sea, where David and later Amaziah won great victories over Edom.
biblical_def: The valley of Salt was a place toward Edom, in the salt waste south of the Dead Sea, the scene of two great victories over the Edomites. There David won renown: “And David gat him a name when he returned from smiting of the Syrians in the valley of salt, being eighteen thousand men” (2Sa 8:13); and there in later days Amaziah king of Judah smote ten thousand of the children of Seir. The valley of Salt preaches the LORD’s subduing of the ancient enemy. Edom, the seed of Esau, was Israel’s perpetual adversary, the brother turned foe, and the prophets foretold his doom; in the valley of Salt the sword of David humbled him, that the word to Rebekah might stand, the elder shall serve the younger. Yet the salt waste warns as well as encourages. When Amaziah won there, he brought home the gods of Edom and bowed to them, and the anger of the LORD was kindled against him, so that his victory turned to his ruin. The valley teaches that triumph over the enemy is dangerous if it puffs up the heart or leads to compromise with the very idols one has vanquished. Let the believer give God the glory of every victory, and beware lest, having overcome, he fall by pride or by embracing the spoils of the foe he was sent to destroy.
